He makes the evacuations according to the inclination of the humours that produce the inflammation; for the precept that one must draw off where it inclines, through the suitable regions, is most true. When, then, the sympathetic affection gives its sign upwards, one must cut a vein at the elbow, the one that is able more, and more quickly, to draw the blood away from the affected part by revulsion and to evacuate it; but when it gives its sign downwards, it is proper to make the evacuation by means of purging. For heaviness, arising as it does from plethora, is a sign that the blood has collected there in greater quantity and is inclining there; but tensions are wont to arise even through sympathetic affection alone, when the parts continuous with the inflamed ones are stretched without the blood being in excess in them. For this very reason, then, he bids one evacuate the excess blood by cutting the inner vein.

The vena cava, carrying the blood up from the convex parts of the liver to the right auricle of the heart, distributes some small amount also to the parts in between, but gives the greatest part to the heart itself. Then, carried from there straight towards the neck, just as it had set out from the beginning, it divides, at the part of the thorax, into two large upright veins, which they call jugular veins. Its offshoots, before it reaches the heart, are large veins into the diaphragm and small ones into the lower part of the thorax itself, the part of the eight ribs, which is nourished by a single azygos vein. In some animals this vein branches off above the heart; in others, as also in human beings, it branches off at the part where the vena cava already touches the auricle of the heart. For, branching off from there, it is carried lower, bending down by way of the heart towards the spine. This vein, then, is distributed into the lower parts of the thorax, to the eight ribs on either side as far as the diaphragm. The remaining four high ribs of the thorax are nourished by another pair of veins, which branch off from the vena cava before it divides into the jugular veins. Next in order after these two veins come those that reach the arms through the armpits. The so-called shoulder veins arise, one from each of the jugulars, after the vena cava has divided into the jugular veins, and they arise already outside the thorax; they have their roots in common with the superficial jugular veins. From the superficial jugular veins, then, nearly all the superficial parts of the neck and the head are nourished, just as all the deep parts are nourished from the deep jugular veins.

Hippocrates himself, then, has taught you the powers of the drugs that he gives in affections of this kind, when he said that black hellebore evacuates things more critical, and that peplion is more apt to break up flatulences.
